scenario.prompt_to_agent:
IT and CS Dept users report they cannot reach Server Room or
Internet Lab. router0 and router2 both report RIP routes intact
and can ping each other's interfaces directly. office_pc (on
router1's own LAN) can still ping its gateway 192.168.3.1, but it
too cannot reach the Server Room. What breaks transit through
router1?

injection.action: drop all transit forwarding on router1 (net.ipv4.ip_forward is not writable from the exec context, so use the iptables equivalent: a FORWARD-chain drop)

scenario.ground_truth:
Affected component: router1 packet forwarding (FORWARD chain)
Mechanism: A FORWARD-chain DROP rule makes router1 drop every
  packet it would route BETWEEN interfaces (transit). Transit
  traffic (it_hod -> router0 -> router1 -> router2 -> pc1) is
  dropped at router1, and office_pc -> Server Room is dropped
  too (it is also transit). Only traffic to router1's OWN
  interfaces still works -- office_pc can still ping its gateway
  192.168.3.1 -- which is the tell that router1 is up but not
  forwarding. RIP keeps running because its sockets are local,
  not forwarded. (This is the iptables equivalent of
  net.ipv4.ip_forward=0, used because that sysctl is not writable
  from the exec context.)
Localization: router1
Root cause: a FORWARD-chain DROP rule on router1 stops transit
  forwarding (equivalent to ip_forward disabled)
Fix: `iptables -D FORWARD -j DROP` on router1 (re-enable forwarding)
scoring_axes: must-identify-component: packet forwarding disabled (FORWARD-chain drop / ip_forward)

agent.diagnosis_text:
Router1 has a blanket iptables DROP rule installed in its FORWARD
chain (rule #1: `-A FORWARD -j DROP`, matching all sources and all
destinations with no interface or protocol restrictions). Because Linux
netfilter processes the FORWARD chain for every packet that the kernel
routes between interfaces, every transit packet entering router1 from
any direction is silently discarded before it can leave on the egress
interface.

This perfectly explains all observed symptoms. IT/CS users (on
router0's LAN, 192.168.1-2.0/24) cannot reach the Server Room
(128.168.0.0/16) or Internet Lab (1.0.0.0/8) behind router2 because
all inter-router transit is blocked at router1. RIP continues to
exchange updates correctly because RIP UPDATE packets are destined to
the router's own interface (INPUT chain, policy ACCEPT — untouched),
so all three routers maintain full routing tables, giving the false
impression that the network is healthy. Similarly, office_pc can ping
its own gateway 192.168.3.1 because that ICMP is handled locally by
router1's INPUT chain; the moment a packet must be forwarded onward,
it hits the FORWARD DROP rule and is discarded. The packet-counter on
the rule visibly incremented from 2 to 5 (by exactly 3) in lockstep
with a 3-packet test ping from office_pc to 128.168.0.2, providing
direct proof.

Root cause: a catch-all `iptables -A FORWARD -j DROP` rule was
injected into router1's FORWARD chain, blackholing all transit traffic.

Corrective fix: on router1, run `iptables -D FORWARD 1` to delete the
offending rule. Transit forwarding will resume immediately without any
routing-protocol restart.
